analysis.one_liner: Forces Apple and Google to let users install apps and rival app stores outside their own stores.
analysis.headline: The bill to break open the Apple and Google app stores has sat untouched in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since September 2025, with no cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any company with more than 100 million U.S. users that owns both a phone operating system and its app store — in practice, Apple and Google — to let users choose default apps and app stores, install apps from outside the official store, and delete preinstalled apps. It would bar those companies from forcing app developers to use their payment systems (where they take up to a 30% cut) or punishing developers who sell elsewhere. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules, with penalties up to $1 million per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Smartphone users, who would get more choice over which apps and app stores they use and could see lower app and subscription prices. App developers — especially makers of streaming, gaming, dating, and subscription apps who now give Apple and Google up to 30% of in-app revenue — would be allowed to use their own payment systems, tell users directly about cheaper offers outside the app, and distribute apps without going through the official store.

how_it_helps.text: Users could set third-party apps and app stores as defaults, install apps from outside the official store, and hide or delete preinstalled apps and stores, on any platform with over 100 million U.S. users [S2].

Apple and Google could no longer require developers to use the platform's own in-app payment system, where commissions run as high as 30%, or forbid developers from offering cheaper prices or terms elsewhere [S2].

Developers could communicate directly with users about prices and offers without paying a fee or facing retaliation, and the platform could not use developers' nonpublic business data to build competing products [S2].

The FTC would enforce the rules as unfair or deceptive practices, with an additional civil penalty of up to $1 million per violation, and state attorneys general could sue on behalf of their residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, whose app stores are the only two major mobile app distribution channels in the U.S. and which collect commissions of up to 30% on in-app purchases and subscription revenue. The bill would cut into that commission income and open their platforms to rival app stores and payment methods.

drawbacks.text: Allowing apps to be installed from outside the official store raises security and privacy risks, since users would be exposed to apps that never passed the platform's review process — the core argument Apple and Google make against such mandates.

The bill preempts state laws that go further: a state could not keep or pass stricter rules requiring the covered companies to allow outside apps or open their platforms, leaving the federal standard as a floor [S2].

The companies must allow outside apps but are not required to warranty, service, or support them, and need not license their intellectual property, so third-party developers may still face practical barriers [S2].

Enforcement depends on the FTC, which must first issue guidance before the law takes effect, and the largest immediate gains could flow to large app developers rather than reaching users as lower prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a genuine two-company bottleneck: nearly every American smartphone runs through Apple's or Google's app store, and both take a cut of in-app sales. Opening that market would likely mean more app choices and downward pressure on subscription and in-app prices, which is why most large app developers favor such rules. The honest costs are real but secondary: sideloading carries added security risk, users absorb that risk themselves, and the bill preempts stricter state-level rules. On balance the design is reasonable — strong federal enforcement, state backup, and exemptions for intellectual property, security, and sanctioned entities — but its benefits to consumers depend on developers actually passing along the commission savings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in September 2025 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat ever since with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and not a single member has signed on as a cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Russell Fry introduced the App Store Freedom Act on September 11, 2025 [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and no further action has been taken [S4].
No member of the House has cosponsored the bill [S3].

The bill would apply only to companies with more than 100 million U.S. users that own both an app store and the operating system it runs on — a definition that currently captures Apple and Google [S2].
The bill would take effect only after the FTC issues compliance guidance, due within 180 days of enactment [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apple and Google are better off so far: with no committee action and no cosponsors, their app-store commissions and control over app distribution face no immediate change. The bill's main effect to date is as a public signal in the broader fight over app-store rules and the government's antitrust cases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Apple and Google, whose stores stay untouched

for.name: Rep. Russell Fry
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the App Store Freedom Act and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: President Trump
for.what_they_did: Publicly said he urged Rep. Fry to introduce the bill, described in reporting as leverage against Apple amid the Justice Department's antitrust case over Google's search business and Apple's App Store practices.

against.name: Rep. Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing or markup has been scheduled.

against.name: Apple
against.role: Operator of the iOS App Store
against.what_they_did: Has opposed app-store mandates like this one, arguing that forcing outside apps and stores onto its platform compromises security and privacy.

against.name: Google (Alphabet)
against.role: Operator of the Google Play Store
against.what_they_did: Has opposed app-store mandates like this one, arguing that outside distribution channels expose users to unsafe apps.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Republican introduced the bill and no one from either party cosponsored it, so no party bloc has taken a position.

industries.industry: Apple and Google (mobile operating systems and app stores)
industries.note: The bill is aimed squarely at these two companies: it would bar them from forcing developers into their payment systems, which take up to a 30% commission, and would let users install rival app stores and delete preinstalled apps. Their control over app distribution and the revenue tied to it is what's at stake.

industries.industry: App developers (streaming, gaming, dating, and subscription apps)
industries.note: Developers could use their own payment systems instead of paying up to 30% to Apple or Google, advertise cheaper offers directly to users, and list apps through other channels. Cheaper distribution makes it more feasible for developers to lower prices for users.

industries.industry: Third-party app stores and payment processors
industries.note: Rival app stores and payment providers would gain a legal right to reach hundreds of millions of U.S. phones, a channel that is now largely closed to them.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee activity since referral, the bill is on the standard path to dying quietly in committee at the end of the Congress. Its most likely real-world role is as public leverage in the fight over Apple's and Google's app-store policies, not as a law that gets enacted — unless the committee leadership decides to move it or it picks up cosponsors.
